claims.text: What the image looks like Dilated blind-ending appendix >6 mm, periappendiceal fat stranding, ± appendicolith → acute appendicitis
claims.quote: Dilated blind-ending appendix >6 mm, periappendiceal fat stranding, ± appendicolith Acute appendicitis

claims.text: Example CT: a dilated, thick-walled appendix (15.31 mm in diameter) with surrounding inflammatory changes
claims.quote: This image shows a dilated, thick-walled appendix (arrows) measuring 15.31 mm in diameter with surrounding inflammatory changes.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Ultrasound: non-compressible blind-ended tubular structure RLQ >6 mm → acute appendicitis (preferred 1st imaging in children, pregnancy)
claims.quote: Non-compressible blind-ended tubular structure RLQ >6 mm Acute appendicitis (preferred 1st imaging in children, pregnancy)
claims.locator: Non-Trauma Ultrasound Findings, Abdomen / Pelvis table

claims.text: KUB: calcified RLQ density (appendicolith) suggests appendicitis → CT with contrast
claims.quote: Calcified RLQ density (appendicolith) Suggests appendicitis CT with contrast

claims.text: Contrast-enhanced CT has good accuracy and can also reveal other causes of an acute abdomen; graded compression ultrasound can usually be done quickly and uses no radiation but is occasionally limited by bowel gas
claims.quote: Contrast-enhanced CT has good accuracy in diagnosing appendicitis (1) and can also reveal other causes of an acute abdomen. Graded compression ultrasound can usually be done quickly and uses no radiation (of particular concern in children); however, it is occasionally limited by the presence of bowel gas and is less useful for recognizing nonappendiceal causes of pain.

claims.text: With classic symptoms and signs the diagnosis is clinical: delaying surgery to do imaging only increases the likelihood of perforation; image without delay when findings are atypical or equivocal
claims.quote: When classic appendicitis symptoms and signs are present, the appendicitis diagnosis is clinical. In such patients, delaying appendicitis surgery to do imaging tests only increases the likelihood of perforation and subsequent complications. In patients with atypical or equivocal findings, imaging studies should be done without delay.

claims.text: Labs typically show leukocytosis (12,000 to 15,000/mcL), but a normal WBC count should not be used to exclude appendicitis
claims.quote: Laboratory studies typically show leukocytosis (12,000 to 15,000/mcL [12.00 to 15.00 × 109/L]), but this finding is highly variable; a normal white blood cell count should not be used to exclude appendicitis.

claims.text: Causes Thought to result from obstruction of the appendiceal lumen, typically by lymphoid hyperplasia but occasionally by a fecalith, foreign body, tumor or worms → distention, bacterial overgrowth, ischemia, inflammation; untreated → necrosis, gangrene, perforation (contained by omentum → appendiceal abscess)
claims.quote: Appendicitis is thought to result from obstruction of the appendiceal lumen, typically by lymphoid hyperplasia but occasionally by a fecalith, foreign body, tumor, or even worms. The obstruction leads to distention, bacterial overgrowth, ischemia, and inflammation. If untreated, necrosis, gangrene, and perforation occur. If the perforation is contained by the omentum, an appendiceal abscess results.

claims.text: Symptoms Classic: epigastric or periumbilical pain followed by brief nausea, vomiting and anorexia; after a few hours the pain shifts to the right lower quadrant; pain increases with cough and motion
claims.quote: The classic acute appendicitis symptoms are Epigastric or periumbilical pain followed by brief nausea, vomiting, and anorexia After a few hours, the pain shifts to the right lower quadrant. Pain increases with cough and motion.

claims.text: Classic sign: RLQ direct and rebound tenderness at the McBurney point; also Rovsing, psoas and obturator signs
claims.quote: Classic signs of appendicitis are Right lower quadrant direct and rebound tenderness located at the McBurney point (junction of the middle and outer thirds of the line joining the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine) Additional appendicitis signs are pain felt in the right lower quadrant with palpation of the left lower quadrant (Rovsing sign), an increase in pain caused by passive extension of the right hip joint that stretches the iliopsoas muscle (psoas sign), or pain caused by passive internal rotation of the flexed thigh (obturator sign).

claims.text: Low-grade fever (rectal 37.7 to 38.3° C) is common; atypical symptoms are common in older patients and pregnant women (pain less severe, local tenderness less marked)
claims.quote: Low-grade fever (rectal temperature 37.7 to 38.3° C [100 to 101° F]) is common. Many variations of appendicitis symptoms and signs occur in > 50% of patients. Pain may not be localized, particularly in infants and children. Tenderness may be diffuse or, in rare instances, absent. Bowel movements are usually less frequent or absent; if diarrhea is a sign, a retrocecal appendix should be suspected. Red or white blood cells may be present in the urine. Atypical symptoms are common among older patients and pregnant women; in particular, pain is less severe and local tenderness is less marked.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: appendectomy; antibiotics if perforated/abscess (drain)
Open or laparoscopic appendectomy; because delay increases mortality, a 15% negative appendectomy rate is considered acceptable
claims.quote: Treatment of acute appendicitis is open or laparoscopic appendectomy. Because treatment delay increases mortality, a negative appendectomy rate of 15% is considered acceptable.

claims.text: Appendectomy should be preceded by IV antibiotics (third-generation cephalosporins preferred); none further for nonperforated appendicitis; continue 4 days if perforated
claims.quote: Appendectomy should be preceded by IV antibiotics. Third-generation cephalosporins are preferred. For nonperforated appendicitis, no further antibiotics are required. If the appendix is perforated, antibiotics should be continued for 4 days (1).

claims.text: Antibiotics alone often resolve the episode, but many recur within a year, so appendectomy is still recommended, particularly if an appendicolith is visible on CT
claims.quote: Although several studies of nonoperative management of appendicitis (ie, using antibiotics alone) have shown high rates of resolution during the initial hospitalization, a significant number of patients have a recurrence and require appendectomy during the following year (2). Thus, appendectomy is still recommended, particularly if an appendicolith is visible on CT.

claims.text: A pericolic abscess is drained by ultrasound-guided percutaneous catheter or open operation, with appendectomy later
claims.quote: In late cases in which a pericolic abscess has already formed, the abscess is drained either by an ultrasound-guided percutaneous catheter or by open operation (with appendectomy to follow at a later date).
